section.title: The Ransomed Shall Return
section.sectionRationale: This short, luminous chapter closes the seam of the final woes and the ransomed return, chapters 33 to 35, answering the desolation of Edom in chapter 34 with a vision of the wilderness itself blossoming, the blind and lame healed, and the ransomed of the LORD walking a highway of holiness home to Zion with everlasting joy.
section.thesis: The same LORD who devotes His enemies to total desolation will just as surely transform the wilderness into a garden, heal the blind and the lame, and bring His ransomed people home along a Way of Holiness, crowned forever with joy that sorrow can never again touch.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the wilderness bursting into bloom; strengthening the weak and fearful; eyes opened and ears unstopped; the highway called the Way of Holiness; and the climactic return of the ransomed to Zion with everlasting joy.

units.label: The wilderness will blossom
units.note: the glory of the LORD revealed

verses.text: The wilderness and the land will be glad; the desert will rejoice and blossom like a rose.
It will bloom profusely and rejoice with joy and singing. The glory of Lebanon will be given to it, the splendor of Carmel and Sharon. They will see the glory of the LORD, the splendor of our God.
Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees!
Say to those with anxious hearts: “Be strong, do not fear! Behold, your God will come with vengeance. With divine retribution He will come to save you.”

units.label: Eyes opened, ears unstopped
units.note: the blind, the lame, the mute

verses.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened and the ears of the deaf unstopped.
Then the lame will leap like a deer and the mute tongue will shout for joy. For waters will gush forth in the wilderness, and streams in the desert.
The parched ground will become a pool, the thirsty land springs of water. In the haunt where jackals once lay, there will be grass and reeds and papyrus.
And there will be a highway called the Way of {{qodesh|Holiness}}. The unclean will not travel it, only those who walk in the Way, and fools will not stray onto it.
No lion will be there, and no vicious beast will go up on it. Such will not be found there, but the redeemed will walk upon it.
So the {{padah|redeemed}} of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy. Gladness and joy will overtake them, and sorrow and sighing will flee.

qodesh.gloss: Holiness, set-apartness. The highway home is named the Way of Holiness because it is reserved for a purified people; the unclean cannot travel it. It anticipates Christ, who does not merely mark the road but calls Himself the Way, John 14:6, the one path by which the unclean are made holy and brought home.

padah.gloss: To redeem or ransom, to free someone by paying a price on their behalf. The redeemed of the LORD are those He Himself has purchased and set free, language that runs through Isaiah's whole Book of Comfort and finds its costliest fulfillment in Christ, who ransoms His people not with silver but with His own blood, 1 Peter 1:18-19.

basic.context: After Edom's desolation in chapter 34, this short chapter turns to glorious hope: the desert will bloom, weak hands and feeble knees will be strengthened, the blind will see and the lame will leap, and a highway called the Way of Holiness will carry the ransomed of the LORD home to Zion with everlasting joy. It is one of the most beautiful visions of restoration in the whole Old Testament.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter first spoke hope to exiles longing to return home, picturing their journey transformed by God's presence, water in the desert, a safe highway, no danger from beasts. Jesus Himself later applies this very language, blind eyes opened, the lame leaping, to His own healing ministry, Matthew 11:4-5, showing that the return from exile was always meant to point toward something greater: the Messiah's own work of healing and restoration.
basic.originalLanguages: The highway is named the Way of {{qodesh}}, holiness, reserved for a purified people alone. Those who walk it are the {{padah}}, the redeemed or ransomed, people bought back at a price. Together the images describe not just a road home but a people made fit to walk it, ransomed and set apart, entering Zion with singing.
basic.typology: The healing of the blind, deaf, lame, and mute anticipates Christ's own miracles, which He explicitly points to as proof of His identity, Matthew 11:4-5. The Way of Holiness anticipates Christ, who calls Himself the Way, the one path to the Father, John 14:6. The everlasting joy that finally banishes sorrow and sighing anticipates the new creation, where God wipes away every tear, Revelation 21:4.
basic.christ: When John the Baptist's disciples ask if Jesus is the Coming One, Jesus answers by pointing to exactly this chapter's signs fulfilled: the blind see, the lame walk, Matthew 11:4-5. Jesus is Himself the Way of Holiness, John 14:6, the one path by which the unclean are cleansed and brought home to God. The everlasting joy promised here, with sorrow and sighing forever fled, is the same joy Revelation 21:4 promises when Christ makes all things new.
basic.god: God is the one who transforms wilderness into blossom and turns weak, fearful people into a strong, singing procession. He comes not merely to punish but to save, opening blind eyes and lame legs as signs of His own presence among His people, and He guarantees that those He has ransomed will reach home, crowned with joy that sorrow can never again touch.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 11:4-5 shows Jesus citing this very chapter's signs as proof of His messianic identity. John 14:6 identifies Jesus as the Way. Revelation 21:4 promises the final wiping away of every tear and the end of sorrow. Isaiah 40:3-5, the next movement, develops the same highway image for the LORD's coming.
basic.oneStory: This chapter's vision of a blooming desert, healed bodies, and a holy highway home is one of Scripture's clearest windows into the whole Bible's hope: God ransoming a broken, exiled people and bringing them home with joy. Jesus fulfills its signs in His own healing ministry and is Himself the Way of Holiness, and its promise of everlasting joy awaits its full completion in the new creation.

context.literary:
Isaiah 35 is short, but it is built with great care, and it is best read as the bright half of a diptych with chapter 34. Where chapter 34 turned Edom's streams to tar and gave the land to owls, chapter 35 sends water into the desert and gives the haunt of jackals to grass and reeds. The two chapters share vocabulary and are arranged as mirror images, which is why the first line of chapter 35 begins with the wilderness 'glad,' as though the ruin of chapter 34 had been the stage for its undoing.

The chapter moves in five steps. Nature rejoices, verses 1 and 2. The weak are told to take heart, verses 3 and 4, the only imperatives in the poem and its pastoral centre. The sick are healed and water flows, verses 5 to 7. A road appears, verses 8 and 9. And a procession arrives, verse 10. The movement is from landscape, to bodies, to road, to people, to the city, so that the whole creation is gathered into one journey.

The names of places link it to the previous chapters. Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon, which verse 9 of chapter 33 had pictured withering, are given to the desert in verse 2. 'Your eyes will see' in 33:17 becomes 'They will see the glory of the LORD' here. The poem is also marked by its pairs, blind and deaf, lame and mute, each of which names an affliction and then reverses it. It ends where the first half of Isaiah is built to end, with Zion, and with a few lines that are repeated almost word for word in 51:11.
context.historical:
The chapter does not name its setting, and that is part of its power. It sits between the Assyrian crisis of chapters 36 and 37, still ahead, and the exile that Isaiah will name in chapter 39, and it speaks to people in either trouble. For Judahites under Assyria's shadow it promised that their land would not stay a battlefield. For exiles in Babylon, who would later read these words as part of the finished scroll, it described a road home across the desert that lay between Mesopotamia and Zion.

That road was real. From Babylon to Jerusalem the shortest routes crossed or skirted hundreds of miles of arid land, and the Syrian desert was the great barrier. A returning company would have thought first of water, of wild animals, and of bandits, which is why the poem names thirst, jackals and lions. When Ezra's company set out they feared the enemy on the road, Ezra 8:21 to 23, and Isaiah's 'no lion will be there' answers fears of exactly that kind.

The healings were not an everyday expectation. Under the law the blind, deaf and lame were excluded from priestly service, Leviticus 21:18, and many were dependent on charity. The promise that they would walk to Zion among the whole company was therefore a promise of full inclusion, not only of cure. The 'unclean' of verse 8 refers to the ritual categories of Leviticus, whose rules defined who could approach the sanctuary, and the poem's road is a pilgrim route with a gatekeeper at its mouth.
context.canonical:
Isaiah 35 has two great echoes. The first is within Isaiah. The central part of the book, chapters 40 to 55, takes up its images again: a highway in the desert, 40:3; streams in the wasteland, 41:18 and 43:19; the exodus-like journey of the redeemed, 48:20 and 52:11 to 12; and the lines of 35:10, which return in 51:11 nearly word for word. The book's last chapters call the returned people 'the Holy People, the Redeemed of the LORD,' 62:12, which draws together the road and its travellers.

The second echo is in the Gospels. When John the Baptist, in prison, sends to ask whether Jesus is the one who was to come, Jesus replies with a list of healings that draws on this chapter along with chapter 61: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, the deaf hear, Luke 7:22. In the Gospels the deaf man who could hardly speak is healed in Mark 7:31 to 37, and the crowd's astonished 'He has done all things well' echoes the creation verdict of Genesis 1:31. In Acts 3:8 a man lame from birth goes in to the temple 'walking and leaping and praising God,' which is the leaping lame of verse 6 in the flesh.

The letter to the Hebrews draws on verse 3 when it tells believers to 'strengthen your limp hands and weak knees,' Hebrews 12:12, applying the prophet's encouragement to people tired of the long road. And the closing line is carried into the last page of Scripture, Revelation 21:4, where God wipes away every tear and sorrow and crying are gone.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The prophet's first aim is to comfort people who have been frightened by the previous chapters. After the long account of woe and judgment he gives them a promise they can hold. The instruction in verses 3 and 4 shows who he thinks the audience is: people with limp hands and anxious hearts, who need someone to say to them, 'Be strong, do not fear.' He does not scold their fear; he gives it a reason.

He also means to draw a map of what restoration includes. It is not only a return of people to a place. It is the renewal of land, bodies and community together: the wilderness blooms, the sick are made whole, the road is made safe, and the whole company arrives in joy. By describing each, he insists that the salvation God brings is as wide as the damage sin has done.

Last, he sets a condition that keeps the poem from sentimentality. The road is holy, and travellers on it are the redeemed, not the wicked or the foolish, verse 8. The promise is for a people who have been set apart by the LORD, and so the chapter, in its gentleness, still insists that holiness is the shape of the life God is leading His people into.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes what God will do, and it commands only one thing, that the strong help the weak: 'Strengthen the limp hands and steady the feeble knees!' That imperative is for the community. Anyone who has taken hold of the promise is given the job of passing it on to the fearful, speaking its words to those who have lost heart, verse 4.

What it does not do is guarantee physical healing to every believer now. The healings of verses 5 and 6 are signs that the kingdom has come near, as Jesus treated them in Luke 7:22, and the full end of sickness waits for the day when sorrow and sighing flee, verse 10. Christians pray for healing and use medicine, and they also live in the hope of a body made new at the resurrection, 1 Corinthians 15:42 to 44. To read the chapter as a promise of present health is to take a down payment for the whole sum.

It also does not say that obedience earns the road. The redeemed walk it because they have been redeemed. The ethical weight of 'the Way of Holiness' describes the shape of the redeemed life, and it is received as gift, as Paul says in Ephesians 2:8 to 10.

debates.question: Is chapter 35 about the return from Babylon, about Christ's ministry, or about the new creation?

views.label: The return from exile
views.case: The language of a road, a procession of the redeemed and entry into Zion with singing matches the homecoming of Isaiah 40 to 55, and the verses are echoed in 51:11 about that return.

views.label: The ministry of Jesus
views.case: Jesus answers John's question by listing signs found in this chapter, Matthew 11:4 to 5. For the Gospels the signs of verses 5 and 6 are visibly happening in Him, and Mark treats the healing of the deaf man as a fulfilment.

views.label: The final restoration
views.case: The wilderness turned to a garden, the end of every danger on the road, and sorrow and sighing fleeing, verse 10, have never happened in full, and Revelation 21:4 places them at the end of history.

debates.bearing: These are best held as stages of one promise. The return gave a pledge, Jesus' healings gave a sign that the kingdom had arrived, and the new creation will give the full measure. The chapter's own wording is wide enough for all three.

debates.question: Who are 'the unclean' and 'fools' who may not use the road in verse 8?

views.label: Ritually and morally impure people, excluded from Zion
views.case: The word 'unclean' is the term of Leviticus for those barred from the sanctuary, and Isaiah 52:1 says the unclean will no longer enter Jerusalem. The road is closed to those who have not been cleansed.

views.label: People who refuse God's way
views.case: The parallel line speaks of 'fools' who stray, and in Proverbs the fool is the one who rejects wisdom. The restriction describes the character of those who choose not to walk the road, not a fixed class of people.

debates.bearing: The two readings agree that the road is for the cleansed and the willing. The gospel then gives the means: those who were unclean are washed, 1 Corinthians 6:11, so that the road is closed only to those who refuse to be made fit.

study.originalLanguages:
The poem opens by piling up words of gladness. The wilderness is 'glad,' the desert 'rejoices' and blossoms, and verse 2 adds 'joy and singing.' Joy language of this kind belongs to Israel's worship, so the dry land is being called into the congregation's song. The verse names the 'rose' (the BSB's choice) among flowers that might surprise a reader expecting only sand, and the point of the line is the surprise.

In verse 2 the poem says that the desert will 'see' the glory of the LORD. The verb is the ordinary one for seeing, and the noun is kavod, glory, a word whose root means weight. The sight of glory in Exodus 16:7 and 40:34 is of the LORD's presence, so here the landscape itself becomes a witness to that presence.

Verse 4 contains a striking pair of nouns: 'vengeance' (naqam) and 'divine retribution' (gemul elohim). The second term is a word for requital, the same word that can describe a good return as well as a bad one, and the BSB's choice of 'retribution' stresses the harsher side. The verse's grammar, however, makes the coming of God the means by which He 'saves' the fearful, so that the very thing that is vengeance for the oppressor is salvation for the oppressed. The verb for save is yasha, the root of Joshua and Jesus.

Verse 5 says 'the eyes of the blind will be opened.' The verb is pakach, 'to open,' which is used elsewhere in Isaiah of the eyes and ears of the people in 42:7 and 42:20, the same two senses in the servant passages. Verse 6's 'mute' translates a word for the speechless and the Septuagint renders a form of it with a rare Greek term that Mark uses for the man in Mark 7:32, 'hardly able to speak,' which suggests that the Gospel writer heard Isaiah 35 in the miracle.

The road of verse 8 is a highway and a way, and the way is called 'the Way of Holiness.' The word for the raised highway, mesillah, comes from a verb meaning to build up, and the same word is used for the prepared road in Isaiah 40:3 and 62:10. The Christians of Acts were called people of 'the Way,' Acts 9:2 and 19:9, and the label may well reflect this Isaianic road.

Finally, verse 10 says 'gladness and joy will overtake them.' The verb is nasag, to overtake or catch up with. The verb is at home in Deuteronomy 28, where blessings 'overtake' the obedient, verse 2, and curses overtake the disobedient, verse 15. Isaiah gives the verb to joy. The people who might have expected curses to run them down find gladness running after them.

typology.type: The healing of the blind, deaf, lame and mute, verses 5 and 6
typology.fulfillment: These healings are signs of God's arrival, and the Gospels show them happening. Jesus heals the blind men, Matthew 9:27 to 31, the deaf man who could hardly speak, Mark 7:31 to 37, and the lame, and tells John's disciples to report what they see, Matthew 11:4 to 5. The correspondence is direct, and the escalation is that the signs now come through one person who is present. The type falls short in the sense that each healed person would eventually die. The healings are previews of the resurrection body and not the final form of it, Romans 8:23.

A single road, open only to the cleansed, leading to Zion. Jesus says 'I am the way and the truth and the life; no one comes to the Father except through Me,' John 14:6. Hebrews describes 'a new and living way' opened for us through the veil of His flesh, Hebrews 10:19 to 22. The road in Isaiah was lawful because it was holy, and in Christ the holiness is supplied rather than demanded. The type falls short in that a physical road leads to a physical city, while Christ leads to the Father Himself.

typology.type: The wilderness turned to a garden, verses 1, 2, 6 and 7
typology.fulfillment: The desert is a standing picture of a creation under curse. Its reversal looks back to Eden, where water watered the garden, Genesis 2:6 and 10, and forward to the river of life, Revelation 22:1 to 2. In the Gospels, Jesus meets the Samaritan woman at a well and offers living water, John 4:10 to 14, and in the desert he feeds thousands, Mark 6:30 to 44, signs of the wilderness giving bread and water. The type falls short because the reversal is only partly seen now, and creation itself still groans, Romans 8:19 to 22.

typology.type: The ransomed company entering Zion with singing, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: A people redeemed at a price, travelling together and arriving with joy. The pattern is that of the exodus, in which the LORD redeemed Israel from Egypt, Exodus 15:13, and the song at the sea, Exodus 15:1. In Christ the redemption price is named: not silver or gold but precious blood, 1 Peter 1:18 to 19. The Revelation's multitude singing before the throne, Revelation 7:9 to 10, is the arrival. The type falls short in that it describes a return to a place, whereas the final arrival is to the presence of God with no temple needed, Revelation 21:22.

study.christ:
Isaiah 35 gives the clearest example in the Old Testament of how Jesus read His own work. When John the Baptist, shaken in prison, sent to ask whether Jesus was the one who was to come, Jesus did not simply say yes. He told the messengers to report what they were seeing and hearing: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, the deaf hear, Matthew 11:4 to 5 and Luke 7:22. That list was an answer drawn from this chapter and from Isaiah 61. John, who knew his Isaiah, would recognise it. The signs of the promised age were no longer promises. Jesus was putting the proof in his hands.

The miracles are therefore more than acts of kindness. In Mark 7 a man who was deaf and could hardly speak is brought to Jesus, and Jesus restores both hearing and speech. The crowd is astonished, and their verdict, 'He has done all things well,' echoes the verdict on the first creation. Isaiah's blind, deaf, lame and mute are the people the Gospels bring to the feet of Jesus one by one. The chapter says that when God comes, these things happen, and the Gospels show them happening in a man's presence. The verse before the healings, 'Behold, your God will come,' verse 4, is thus answered in a way Isaiah's first readers could not have guessed.

The Way of Holiness is also fulfilled in Him. A road that the unclean cannot walk is a problem for everyone, since all are unclean, Romans 3:23. Jesus is the way that makes it possible. He does not point to a path; He is the path, John 14:6, and He opens it by cleansing: 'you were washed, you were sanctified,' 1 Corinthians 6:11. The ransomed of verse 10 are those He has redeemed with His own blood, Ephesians 1:7, and the everlasting joy with which they are crowned is joy He shares with them, John 15:11.

Verse 4 is worth noticing too. It says God 'will come with vengeance' and 'to save you' in the same sentence. For those who know Christ, the cross is where both are true. The vengeance on sin and the salvation of sinners meet in one event, Romans 3:25 to 26, so that the grammar of Isaiah 35:4 becomes the story of Good Friday.

A guard against over-reading: the chapter says nothing about a suffering Messiah, and its original audience would have thought of the LORD's own coming. The link to Jesus runs through the Gospels' own use of its language and through their claim that in Him the LORD has come.
study.god:
The God of Isaiah 35 is a God who transforms. He does not merely rescue people from a bad place and leave the place as it was. The wilderness itself is changed, and the land is given the splendour of Lebanon, Carmel and Sharon, places proverbial for beauty and abundance. Salvation in the Bible is never only about souls; it reaches the soil and the body. The God who made the world as a garden has not forgotten what He made, and verses 1 to 7 are a sort of creation song sung in the future tense.

He is also a God who attends to the weakest. The hands that are limp and the knees that are feeble are not first addressed as a problem; they are encouraged. The first commandment of the chapter is a pastoral one, to strengthen them, and the reason is God's own coming. The Lord who is mighty enough to scatter armies in chapter 34 is gentle enough in chapter 35 to meet a trembling man and tell him not to fear. The chapter does not set these side by side as a contradiction, since a person who fears is helped by knowing that the one who comes is stronger than what he fears.

God is, again, holy, and does not apologise for it. The road that He builds has a character, and those who walk it are His. Holiness here is not an obstacle in His way to sinners; it is the nature of the road He makes for them. His redeemed are 'redeemed of the LORD,' a phrase that places the initiative and the cost with Him. The word for redeem has two relatives here, one the word for the kinsman who buys back, the other the word for paying a ransom, and both fit a God who acts as a family member who will not abandon His own, and who pays what it costs.

Finally, He is the God of joy. The chapter's last line does not end with 'and they were safe' but with sorrow and sighing fleeing and gladness overtaking them. A God who says 'Be strong, do not fear' is not only commanding but offering something. In worship the result is that praise is not an add-on to belief; it is the shape that the believing life will have when it arrives. Christians sing now, in the wilderness, as the first company of the ransomed, and the song is a rehearsal for the final arrival. The One who ransoms is the One who finishes: there is no stranded traveller on this road.

crossReferences.note: Jesus tells John's messengers to report what they see and hear: the blind receive sight, the lame walk, the deaf hear. He answers the question 'Are You the One who was to come?' by pointing to the signs of Isaiah 35:5 to 6 as now taking place. It is the New Testament's own proof that this chapter's promises have begun to come true in Him.

A deaf man who could hardly speak is healed, and the astonished crowd says that He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak. The scene reads as Isaiah 35:5 and 35:6 in a single event, showing the Gospel writer's habit of telling Jesus' miracles in the light of the prophets' promises.

A man lame from birth is healed at the temple gate by the name of Jesus, and he enters the temple walking, leaping and praising God. The leaping lame man of Isaiah 35:6 appears in flesh, in the place of Zion, which shows that the apostles' work continues the signs that Jesus began.

A voice cries to prepare the way of the LORD in the wilderness and to make a highway in the desert for our God. The road that is the Way of Holiness in 35:8 is now prepared for the LORD's own coming, and all four Gospels apply it to John the Baptist and to Jesus.

The redeemed of the LORD will return and enter Zion with singing, crowned with everlasting joy, and gladness will overtake them. It repeats the last verse of chapter 35 almost word for word, now as the confident prayer of those awaiting the exodus from Babylon, showing how the promise was held and handed on.

The land mourns and languishes, Lebanon is ashamed, Sharon is like a desert, Bashan and Carmel shake off their leaves. The same names are turned around in 35:2, where Lebanon's glory and the splendor of Carmel and Sharon are given to the desert, so that the poem answers the ruin of chapter 33 directly.

Edom's towers are overgrown, and the land becomes a haunt for jackals and ostriches. Isaiah 35:7 speaks of the haunt where jackals once lay becoming grass, reeds and papyrus. The echo is deliberate: what judgment ruined in one chapter, God redeems in the next.

Believers are told to strengthen their limp hands and weak knees and to make straight paths for their feet, so that the lame may not be put out of joint but healed. This takes Isaiah 35:3 and applies it to a church that is tired, so that the prophet's encouragement becomes pastoral advice in the New Testament.

God will wipe away every tear, and there will be no more death or mourning or crying or pain. The end of sorrow and sighing in Isaiah 35:10 is here given its full scale, with God dwelling among His people, and the old order of things has passed away.

The people are told to go out through the gates, build up the highway and clear it of stones, and are called the Holy People, the Redeemed of the LORD. It develops the image of 35:8 to 10 into a call for the community to prepare the road and a name for those who travel it.

study.oneStory:
Isaiah 35 sits between a wrecked world and a restored one, and that is the shape of the whole Bible. The story begins in a garden with water, trees and a close walk with God, Genesis 2. It goes wrong in Genesis 3, and the result is thorns, thistles and exile from the presence, 3:18 and 24. The word 'wilderness' has been the biblical name for the world outside the garden ever since. Israel crosses a wilderness on the way out of Egypt, wanders in one, and is carried off into one by exile. In this chapter the wilderness, which has stood for all of that, is told to be glad.

What this answers from before is a long ache. Eden was closed, and the way back was barred by a flaming sword. The exodus gave Israel a road and a God who went with them, Exodus 13:21, but the people never reached the rest it promised, Hebrews 3:7 to 19. Here, at last, the road is a highway that is safe, and nobody goes astray on it. The promise to Abraham that his family would bless the nations, Genesis 12:3, is still waiting, and the redeemed company of the chapter, called from near and far, is the shape of it.

What it sets up is the second half of Isaiah and the work of the Servant. After this joyful end to the first part, the book will go on to the Babylonian exile, and then to the comfort that begins in chapter 40. The picture of a road for the redeemed is the promise that will be unfolded by one who is despised and rejected, and wounded for transgressions, 53:3 to 5. That is the paradox: the road of joy is paved with the Servant's suffering. The gladness that overtakes the redeemed is paid for.

In the end the New Testament answers every part of it. Jesus opens the eyes of the blind and calls Himself the Way. The Spirit is the living water that Jesus promised, John 7:37 to 39, and the church, called 'the Way,' walks in it. The last chapters of Revelation give the arrival: a city, a river, a tree, the nations walking by its light, and no more curse, Revelation 22:1 to 3. Isaiah 35 is thus a travel poem for the whole people of God, a promise from the middle of the story that the story will end well, and that those who set out on the road in faith will come home singing.

quiz.q: What transformation does the wilderness undergo in verses 1 to 2?

options.text: It becomes glad and blossoms like a rose, sharing in the glory of Lebanon, Carmel, and Sharon.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2 describe exactly this transformation of the wilderness into abundant, glorious bloom.

options.text: It remains barren but becomes safer to travel through.
options.note: The passage describes active flourishing and blossoming, not mere safety amid continued barrenness.

options.text: It is destroyed entirely and replaced by ocean.
options.note: The opposite; the wilderness blossoms and rejoices rather than being destroyed.

options.text: It becomes a permanent desert with no vegetation at all.
options.note: The text describes the desert rejoicing and blooming profusely, the reverse of permanent barrenness.

quiz.q: What signs of healing are promised in verses 5 to 6?

options.text: The blind will see, the deaf will hear, the lame will leap, and the mute will sing for joy.
options.note: These verses list exactly this set of healings, later cited by Jesus as messianic signs.

options.text: Only emotional comfort is promised, with no mention of physical healing.
options.note: The text specifically names physical conditions: blindness, deafness, lameness, and muteness.

options.text: Healing is promised only for children, not adults.
options.note: No such age restriction appears in the text; the healing is described generally.

options.text: The healings are limited to a select few religious leaders.
options.note: The text describes these signs as characterizing the whole restored community, not a select religious class.

quiz.q: Who may travel the highway called the Way of Holiness, according to verse 8?

options.text: Only those who walk in the Way; the unclean and fools will not travel it.
options.note: Verse 8 states this restriction directly, reserving the highway for the redeemed alone.

options.text: Anyone at all, regardless of moral or spiritual condition.
options.note: The verse specifically excludes the unclean and fools from this highway.

options.text: Only the wealthy elite of Jerusalem.
options.note: The qualification given is holiness and cleanness, not wealth or social status.

options.text: Only trained travelers with special equipment.
options.note: The qualification is moral and spiritual purity, not practical travel skill.

quiz.q: How does Jesus use the healing imagery of this chapter in the Gospels?

options.text: He points to the blind seeing and the lame walking as proof He is the promised Messiah, in answer to John the Baptist.
options.note: Matthew 11:4-5 records Jesus doing exactly this, directly echoing Isaiah 35.

options.text: He rejects this chapter as irrelevant to His ministry.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus directly applies this chapter's language to His own works.

options.text: He applies it only to a future, entirely different prophet.
options.note: Jesus applies it to His own present ministry, not to another future figure.

options.text: He uses it only as a metaphor with no connection to actual miracles.
options.note: Jesus points to His literal healing miracles as the fulfillment, not merely a metaphor.

quiz.q: What is promised about sorrow in the chapter's closing verse, verse 10?

options.text: Gladness and joy will overtake the ransomed, and sorrow and sighing will flee.
options.note: Verse 10 gives this exact promise as the climax of the chapter.

options.text: Sorrow will increase even as the people return home.
options.note: The opposite; sorrow and sighing are promised to flee, not increase.

options.text: Joy and sorrow will remain permanently mixed together.
options.note: The verse promises sorrow's flight, not a permanent mixture with joy.

options.text: Only some of the ransomed will experience this joy.
options.note: The promise is given to the whole company of the ransomed entering Zion, not a select few.

questions: The desert is promised to blossom and rejoice. Where in your life feels like a wilderness right now, and how does this promise shape your hope for it?
Verse 3 calls for strengthening limp hands and feeble knees. Who around you needs that kind of encouragement, and what would it look like for you to offer it this week?
Jesus pointed to blind eyes opened and lame legs healed as proof of who He is. Where do you need fresh confidence that Jesus is exactly who He claims to be?
Only the redeemed can walk the Way of Holiness. What does it mean for you personally that you walk this way not by your own effort but because you have been ransomed by Christ?
The chapter promises that sorrow and sighing will flee before everlasting joy. What sorrow are you carrying that you need to entrust to the God who promises this final joy?

translationNotes.note: This healing language is directly cited by Jesus in Matthew 11:4-5 as evidence of His messianic identity, making this one of Isaiah's clearest advance windows into the Gospel accounts.
This verse recurs almost verbatim at Isaiah 51:11, showing how central this image of joyful, sorrow-free homecoming is to the book's larger hope.
